Before you start

Nobody shares which accounts they follow or where they applied. If a student seems to be struggling with how they see their body, connect them with a counselor afterward.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why comparing to a feed feels worse than reality (the highlight filter and hidden struggle), use a four-question check on a post that stings, and choose one change to what they see.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 4 minHow many felt left out or behind this week?
  2. 6 minThe highlight filter, and likes are contagious
  3. 10 minThe four-question check, practiced on a post: turn and talk, share out
  4. 5 minPrivate account audit
  5. 10 minThree moments: December, Jay, Riley
  6. 5 minStarting lines, and comparison you didn’t pick (private)
  7. 5 minWhere else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The guess, the highlight filter, the four-question check on a post, one of the three moments, and the close.

Before you teach
Seniors in decision season.

In December and March, acceptance posts hit hard. Don't ask anyone to share where they applied or heard back.

Body comparison is close to the surface.

The fitness-account example can land hard for students with eating concerns. Keep it about the feeling and the inputs, never weights or bodies. If a student seems to be struggling, connect them with a counselor afterward.

Keep the audit private.

Nobody shares which accounts they follow or mute. The card goes home with them.

Families compare differently.

In some families, comparing to a sibling or cousin is how high hopes get said out loud. In others it never comes up. Present both as normal. The reflection is private.

Don't preach quitting social media.

Most students won't, and the research supports limits and better inputs, not only full breaks. Meet them there.

If someone is being targeted online.

Bullying or threats are a counselor conversation that day, not a discussion topic.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

"Is it a fair match?" carries the equity piece.

Some students work, care for siblings, or have no paid summer options. Name that work as building something real (Jay's scenario), so the lesson doesn't treat a paid program as the standard.

Families compare in different ways.

Openly comparing to siblings or cousins is how some families show high hopes; others never mention achievement. Present both as normal and keep the reflection private. Avoid "In X families" generalizations.

Who students see in their feeds.

Students of color, LGBTQ+ students and disabled students may rarely see people like them, or may see them mocked. Following creators who share your identity is a valid "keep." Harassment aimed at identity is a counselor conversation that day.

Bodies.

Keep every example about the after-feeling, never weight or shape. Students of every size and ability are in the room.

Not everyone is online.

Some families limit social media for religious, family or money reasons. Let those students apply the four questions to school, sports or family comparisons.

No cost to any of the moves.

Muting, hiding like counts and app limits are built into phones and apps. Nothing in the lesson requires a paid tool.

What the research says

People judge themselves by comparing to others, especially when there's no objective measure. For most of history the comparison group was a few dozen people you knew.

Festinger, 1954

In a simulated Instagram feed, photos with more likes activated teens' reward circuitry, and teens were more likely to like photos that already had many likes, including risky ones.

Sherman et al., Psychological Science, 2016 (UCLA)

People consistently underestimate how often peers feel sad, lonely or anxious. Those who underestimated more reported more loneliness.

Jordan et al., 2011 (Stanford)

Heavier Facebook users had lower self-esteem, explained by exposure to people who seemed to be doing better. Viewing one upbeat profile lowered how people felt about themselves.

Vogel et al., 2014

143 college students limited Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to 10 minutes each per day for three weeks and reported less loneliness and fewer depression symptoms. Small sample, a strong hint rather than the final word.

Hunt et al., 2018 (Penn)

Young women who saw "Instagram vs reality" pairs felt better about their bodies than those who saw only the posed photos.

Tiggemann and Anderberg, 2020
